Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 

# Appendix A Industrial and economic outlook, 2012-16 

## 1.  Risks mount in the Eurozone and China 

The Eurozone is back where it was at the end of 2011, with the added burden of greatly amplified political uncertainty.  The election in Greece on 6 May completed the unravelling triggered by Spain’s reappraisal of its budgetary outlook in April.  Even though Greece’s second election on 17 June gave pro-euro parties a smell majority, some sort of Greek default remains very probable, with an increased risk that the event will be chaotic.  Indeed, the mounting pressure on the Spanish banking system indicates that contagion is at work already. 

We now assume Greece’s default will be disorderly, but our base case assumes also that the Eurozone leadership takes measures sufficient to avoid the worst contagion effects.  The risk that they fail to do this, however, we rate at close to 50%.  Preliminary analysis indicates that the Eurozone would suffer a recession at least as severe as in 2009 in this case.  Meanwhile the Eurozone ex Germany wants to tilt its policy mix more towards growth, but Germany is unlikely to agree to more deficit financing.  So policy changes are likely to be more about rhetoric than substance in the short term, and yield incremental benefits at most.  Thus the main uncertainties are less to do with whether Greece defaults, but more to do with how and when.  A make or break debt repayment is due on 20 August, so the moment of truth is getting closer. 

Meanwhile China’s April data releases were disappointing, and suggested that activity continued to decelerate into the second quarter.  Indeed, it provided something of a wake-up call for policy makers.  Fortunately, Chinese inflation slowed also, so the authorities now have large scope to rejuvenate growth.  We assume they will act promptly and, following the recent 50 basis point cut in the Required Reserve Ratio (RRR), policy statements indicate a clear tilt towards growth.  We have therefore pushed the turning point in this cycle no further out than the middle of the year, and expect growth to begin accelerating in the second half of 2012. 

Overall we have held our base case roughly steady.  Our aggregate growth rates are only basis points different from three months ago.  But the divergence within our Eurozone forecast has increased significantly.  The key conclusion we have drawn, however, is that following the first Greek election the outlook is just about as uncertain as it’s been since 2008 and 2009.

## 2.  Regional developments 

### 2.1  The Americas: USA a bastion of (modest) growth 

Compared with the Eurozone the USA is a bastion of growth, albeit modest growth.  As expected GDP expanded at a decelerating rate in the first quarter, by 2.2% annualised quarteron-quarter, down from 3% in the final three months of 2011.  Consumption made the biggest contribution, followed by stock building.  The majority of high frequency data indicate that growth is holding up, despite the headwinds from across the Atlantic, much as we expect it to, and as a result we have held our forecast fairly steady this month.  But the outlook is not without its risks, and these may be a little more acute now. 

Activity fluctuates from month to month, but the underlying trend remains positive. Industrial production increased by 1.1% month-on-month in April, following a more volatile performance in the preceding two months.  As a result the three month on three month rate of output growth slowed to a still healthy 7.5% annualised from almost 10% in March.  The April performance lifted the capacity utilisation rate to 79.2%, its highest reading in four years, and only one percentage point shy of its long-run average.  Manufacturing output increased by 0.6%, led by another solid gain in vehicle production.  What is more the Institute of Supply Management’s manufacturing index is signalling further modest output growth in the near term. But modest is all it will be – core orders for durable goods excluding aircraft were flat monthon-month in March, signalling meagre times ahead for some sectors. 

Although domestic demand is

expanding at a moderate pace, US industry is being helped by improvements in competitiveness versus most other developed economies and China.  As a result two thirds of US manufacturers have moved facilities in the last two years, and the USA has been the top destination to relocate to.  Looking out to 2013, however, the effects of weak demand for US exports this year, in particular in the Eurozone, is likely to detract from output growth as firms subsequently reduce their inventories. 

More encouraging still, housing starts picked up in April after falling in February and March, by 2.6% month-on-month to an annualised rate of 717,000 units.  The upturn was led by a surge in the construction of apartments for rental, because so many would-be first time buyers are opting to rent at present as they prefer to pay down their student loans before saving for a deposit.  It will be many quarters before construction makes the sort of contribution to GDP growth we grew accustomed to prior to the financial crisis, but because activity is growing from a very low base the sector is starting to recover strongly on trend measures: residential construction spending in the first quarter rose at an annual rate of 19%, and the dearth of properties to let is likely to fuel activity further.  Certainly, house prices measured by the CaseShiller index stabilised in March, after 10 months of falls. 

Nonetheless the recovery remains fundamentally modest in nature and that is most evident in the labour market.  The USA created only 115,000 net new non-farm jobs in April.  This was the slowest rate of job formation in six months, and a significant deceleration from the rate around the turn of the year.  The unemployment rate edged lower to 8.1% from 8.2% in March, but that was thanks to the participation rate falling back to a 30 year low.  Critically the jobs market is too fragile to make inroads into long-term unemployment to any significant extent.

145 

We are confident job gains will continue to outstrip job losses: the ratio of unemployed people to each job vacancy has fallen to its lowest since November 2008, and productivity growth has slumped to a crawl.  But we are less confident that the unemployment rate will fall back towards readings consistent with full employment any time soon: private sector gains are likely to be offset by a pick-up in federal layoffs once the spending cuts kick in, in 2013.  That is why we have the unemployment rate in excess of 5% right out to 2016. 

Households remain justifiably cautious.  Consumer spending is holding up, just.  It inched ahead by 0.1% month-on-month in March, even though consumer credit increased at its fastest rate in five months.  Retail sales ex autos, gasoline and building materials increased 0.4% month-on-month in April, so consumers may have made a more solid start to the second quarter. Indeed, the University of Mich

igan’s index of consumer sentiment increased to 77.8 in May, from 76.4 in April, its highest reading since January 2008.  Critically, however, wages continue to stagnate if not fall marginally in real terms so, unless households are going to return to their minimal savings habits of 4-5 years ago, which we think unlikely, the main impetus to consumer spending has to come from increases in the size of the salaried and waged labour force, and as we have seen, those are likely to remain moderate for some time yet. 

So far the US economy has managed to insulate itself from the worst effects of the slowmotion crisis in Europe.  What is more, the Federal Reserve has recently indicated that it stands ready to implement more quantitative easing in the event of a shock.  However, the USA is exposed to risks arising from its own indebtedness, and these are coming to the fore again.  The debt ceiling agreed in 2011 is likely to be reached at the end of 2012, on present trends, or early 2013, if the Treasury implements extraordinary measures again.  Therefore, within the next 7-10 months or so, a new debt ceiling will have to be negotiated in Congress. 

Recently the Speaker of the House of Representatives has signalled that a further increase in the ceiling will have to be accompanied by significant additional spending cuts.  Other things remaining equal, however, $560-570 billion in tax increases (as temporary cuts expire) and spending cuts, equal to 3-4% of GDP in full, are likely to take effect on 1 January 2013, unless a new deficit compact is agreed.  The Republican majority in the House of Representatives intends to vote to extend the temporary tax cuts before the presidential election in November, thereby creating the need for even larger spending cuts unless the borrowing ceiling is lifted. There is a risk, therefore, of a replay of last summer’s debt brinkmanship around the turn of the year.  More generally we assume that some of the temporary tax cuts will be extended again, but we also assume that the tranche of spending cuts mandated last November are implemented as well, which is why we have growth remaining sluggish in 2013.  The possibility of much deeper spending cuts poses appreciable downside risk to the outlook, however. 

Despite a raft of government stimulus measures, Brazil’s economy contracted in each of the first three months of the year.  The latest month-on-month contraction of 0.35% in March was driven by a fall in the industrial sector which has become increasingly uncompetitive due to an inflated exchange rate and high domestic costs.  Real GDP grew only 1.1% in the first quarter, following disappointing 1.0% growth in the fourth as a result. 

With the slowdown persisting in spite of a sustained cycle of aggressive cuts in the central bank benchmark lending rate, the recovery appears now to be more sluggish than previously

anticip

ated.  Not only has the Central Bank’s benchmark interest rate, the Selic, been cut to near-historical lows, the Brazilian real has fallen over 18% against the dollar since early February as investor sentiment has shifted away from riskier emerging markets.  Both the weakening currency and a fall in the policy rate were welcomed by manufacturers but neither has been sufficient to reverse last year’s slowdown as yet. 

Domestic industry, for example, continues to disappoint with survey data such as the HSBC manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) suggesting a softening manufacturing outlook.  The index fell to 49.3 in April from 51.1 in March on the back of a reduction in both output and new orders.  The reading signals a contraction in activity in the industrial sector in part due to the ongoing weakness in the global economy but also a surge in imports from China. 

While manufacturing has continued to be undermined by external demand, domestic demand seems to be easing also.  Unemployment is at record low levels and wages have been driven up by recent minimum wage increases but consumers are already overstretched.  An 8% year-onyear fall in the demand for credit in the first quarter suggests that credit-fuelled consumer growth may be slowing.  This indicates that, at prevailing interest rates, Brazilians currently have a preference for paying down existing debt. 

To be sure, the Brazilian authorities are walking a tightrope.  Insufficient or misdirected stimulus and manufacturing will continue to labour as it has done recently.  Too much intervention may restart inflation, forcing Brazil again to raise interest rates and attract speculative foreign inflows.  Furthermore, while interest rate and exchange rate manipulation contributes to short-term stability, interventions will only be successful in the long term if the underlying fundamentals are supportive.  Although the near-term recovery appears now to be more sluggish, we still expect further fiscal and monetary stimulus measures gradually to reignite growth.  As such, we have made very little change to our outlook.  We forecast growth of about 3% this year, followed by a sharp recovery in 2013 to around 4.7%.  The major risk to the forecast is a further deterioration in the Eurozone, causing global risk aversion to weigh on both domestic and foreign demand. 

### 2.2  Europe: less whether Greece defaults, more how/when 

The prospect of a disorderly Greek default and possible exit from the Eurozone has intensified following the results of the Greek general election on 6 May, which saw an inconclusive result with a strong representation of anti-bailout parties.  Even though these parties did less well in the 17 June re-run, this was only because the pro-euro caucus talked of renegotiating the country’s bail-out measures too.  The financial consequences of this political stalemate have already started manifesting themselves in rising Spanish and Italian bond yields, and a slow motion

bank run in Cyprus and elsewhere on the Eurozone’s periphery.  Meanwhile, France’s new Socialist president, Franзois Hollande, has pledged to prioritise growth over austerity.  However, his plans are likely to face stiff opposition from Angela Merkel, who is determined to force the periphery to stick to their strict spending plans.  Germany represents the biggest upside surprise to our forecast this month, where activity rose by much more than expected in the first quarter of 2012.  However this was countered by an even more recessionary periphery.

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Appendix A 

147 

Popular disquiet with fiscal austerity found a voice in the 6 May elections in Greece and France.  France’s new Socialist president, Franзois Hollande, has pledged to renegotiate the EU fiscal compact (which currently espouses strict spending limits) in order to prioritise growth. However he is likely to face opposition from Angela Merkel, who is unlikely to significantly soften her stance.  Despite recent electoral setbacks in North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Germany’s biggest state with 18 million inhabitants, Mrs Merkel’s personal approval ratings remain high, and opinion polls show the majority of Germans support her European strategy, which they see as the best way to limit the impact of the crisis on their personal finances.  Mrs Merkel will also find it difficult to backtrack on fiscal austerity considering the efforts made to push the agenda in the other peripheral economies. 

Meanwhile, Hollande may have won some support at the latest G-8 summit for his progrowth ideas.  However, such backsliding on austerity would effectively rule out a sufficiently robust fiscal union to allow the north to countenance a common Eurobond for example (something he has been pushing for).  Also, on a more fundamental basis, Hollande will find it difficult to fund his spending plans.  If they are financed by borrowing, they are likely to raise borrowing costs, hurting the economy; if they are financed by offsetting tax increases, or by a reprioritisation of spending (i.e. are fiscally neutral) then they will have a limited growth impact. 

Meanwhile, Greece's political landscape has been in disarray since its inconclusive election on 6 May left parliament divided between supporters and opponents of the €130 billion EU/IMF bailout, with neither side able to form a government.  With the country set to run out of money as early as 20 August and no government in place to negotiate the next aid tranche, the prospect of a disorderly default has increased significantly compared to last month, and now constitutes our base case.  And, because the political situation is so uncertain, with negotiations likely to take place between the new Greek government and the EU/ECB/IMF (troika), the timing of this event is highly uncertain as it depends on what compromises (if any) can be made between both parties.  However, the knock-on effe

cts of this political stalemate have already manifested themselves in the financial sector.  Worries about a run on Greek banks have rattled Athens, with savers withdrawing at least €700 million on 14 May alone.  Data show depositors have also taken flight from banks in Belgium, France, Spain and Italy.  This presents the forecast with another significant risk – that financial markets overrule any political decisions, and force Greece to undertake an early departure. 

Ten-year bond yields are also hovering above the crucial 6% level in Spain and Italy, as investors grow more fearful amidst news of bank credit-rating downgrades and worsening public finances.  Nowhere is this felt more keenly than in Spain, where heroic efforts have been made to knock the Spanish budget into shape after the battering it has received, principally from the banks, but also from its regions.  Unfortunately the problem has escalated at a pace that outstrips Spain’s ability and capacity to introduce new measures.  This was amply illustrated by recent news that Spain’s final deficit figure for 2011 was revised up to 8.9% from the originally reported 8.5%, largely thanks to upward revisions in three regions.  The EU-agreed target had been 6%.  Spain’s banking problems may push Mrs Merkel to allow the EU bailout fund to directly recapitalise faltering European banks, bypassing lending to governments (which adds to a nation’s sovereign debt), essentially solving one problem by creating another.

148 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Appendix A 

Our base case assumes limited contagion effects to the rest of the Eurozone economy following a Greek default and possible exit.  However, the downside risk of significant contagion is large because the bailout fund is generally seen as inadequate and financial markets could interpret a Greek exit as a damning verdict on the Eurozone itself.  We also see limited upside risk from the shift to a more pro-growth agenda, mainly because Mrs Merkel will be opposed to anything significant i.e. anything that involves more bailout funds coming from German taxpayers, or higher German borrowing costs coming from the introduction of Eurobonds for example. 

Germany represents the biggest upside surprise to our forecast this month, where activity rose by 0.5% quarter-on-quarter in the first quarter of 2012 compared with the consensus forecast of a 0.1% increase.  Not only did industrial production rise 2.8% in March, as milder weather helped construction output rebound, but new orders and the Ifo index also improved. Orders for capital goods from outside Europe have improved particularly strongly.  Recent retail sales figures have shown a degree of moderate improvement, reflecting historically low unemployment and stabilising consumer confidence, although this may reverse if events in the Eurozone take a turn for the worse.  Overall we now forecast German growth of 0.8% this year, and 1.1% in 2013.

The overall threat of a Greek default has pushed the euro well below $1.30, and is likely to assist Germany’s export sector, creating further divergences between Germany and the rest.  In terms of the first quarter GDP activity data, these divergences are clearly evident.  While Austria and Belgium posted modest quarterly gains, French GDP stagnated.  Meanwhile, Italian GDP dropped by 0.8%, Spanish GDP fell by 0.3% and the Dutch economy contracted by 0.2%. Portuguese GDP fell by only 0.1%, but after an extremely sharp contraction in the final quarter of 2011.  Available data paint a similar picture for Greece. 

Looking ahead, the region remains worryingly reliant on growth in Germany and a renewed Eurozone contraction is likely to begin in the second quarter.  The manufacturing and services PMIs fell sharply in April, and both are clearly in contraction territory.  Fiscal austerity will continue to dampen growth; unemployment has yet to peak and credit conditions beyond Germany remain very tight. 

The European Central Bank (ECB) held interest rates in May and signalled no change is likely in the foreseeable future.  However, with the bond markets showing signs of deteriorating again following the LTRO-fuelled pickup of early 2012, the ECB is likely to intervene in secondary markets once more.  However, Mrs Merkel has ruled out making unlimited purchases, which could prove futile anyway if financial markets decide the Eurozone project is doomed following a Greek default and exit. 

Overall, we have not significantly changed our forecast this month because we cut our forecasts aggressively in December 2011 to factor in an inevitable Greek default.  However, what has changed is that we now assume this default will be disorderly, and therefore the downside risks are larger because there is a higher chance that this type of event will spark off contagion in the rest of the European economy which runs out of control.  Furthermore, the better than expected performance of Germany this year will be countered by an even more

recessionary periphery.  We now forecast -0.9% growth in the Eurozone this year, and stagnation in 2013. 

Meanwhile, in the UK the preliminary estimate of GDP for the first quarter of 2012 reported a surprise 0.2% quarter-on-quarter contraction which meant the economy was back in a technical recession.  The main reason for this fall was a sharp decline in construction output (down 3% on the quarter) and a dip in services activity.  However, given the wide divergence between the GDP series and a whole range of other indicators, including business surveys and official labour market data, we expect it to be revised upwards at a later date. 

Looking ahead, headline growth rates are likely to be bumpy with extra public holidays in the second quarter, and the hosting of the Olympic Games in the third quarter.  But there is likely to be a pi

ck-up in underlying activity.  The consumer outlook is beginning to improve; with the labour market showing signs of stabilisation, and renewed declines in oil prices promise a sharp drop in inflation.  We also expect the contributions from business investment and net exports to strengthen somewhat as the year progresses.  Overall, we now forecast growth of 0.3% this year, and 1.5% in 2013. 

Russia’s economy grew 4.9% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2012, defying expectations that a cooling global economy would sap growth.  This was mostly driven by a surge in consumption, explained by government expenditure before parliamentary and presidential elections, as well as residual post-crisis economic stimulus spending. 

However, most evidence suggests that economic growth is now starting to flag.  Oil prices have fallen and Russia’s stock market has slumped 20% since March, erasing its gains over the year.  Capital flight also surged in the first quarter, totalling $35.1 billion, compared with about $80 billion in 2011 overall.  This was blamed partly on political instability in the run-up to the 4 March elections.  Retail sales growth fell in April, and industrial output growth was just 1.3% during the same month, as the global economic slowdown bit into the export sector.  Furthermore, the expected mid-year rise in utility prices will eat away at real spending power, with retail loan growth also bound to moderate from current high levels.  We now expect growth of 4.2% this year, and 3.4% in 2013.  The main downside risk to this forecast remains the fact that economic turmoil in Europe is expected to hit Russia particularly hard. 

Similarly, most countries in Central and Eastern Europe rely overwhelmingly on demand from the EU.  Poland, Romania, Hungary and the Czech Republic are all likely to have recorded falls in industrial output in the first quarter of 2012.  In the case of the latter two this will mean declining GDP given the weakness of domestic demand, which is under pressure from fiscal austerity.  Furthermore, the outlook could easily worsen if the Eurozone recession is deeper and/or persists for longer than expected or prompts a renewed bout of financial turmoil (which would lead to a further tightening of credit conditions). 

### 2.3  Asia: April data give a wake-up call to China’s policy makers 

The promising signs in the March data that the Chinese economy had bottomed and that prospects were beginning to improve were well and truly shaken with the release of a slew of surprisingly bad official data for April.  While anecdotal evidence and surveys point to a flat to 

CRU International Limited confidential 

150 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Appendix A 

improving trajectory in the economy, the official data for trade, industrial output, investment and construction all posted slower year-on-year growth. 

The timing of the Qing Ming holiday meant that there were fewer working days in April this year compared with last

and that will have been a contributory factor in the weaker comparisons with 2011.  However, retail sales, which should have received a boost from the additional holiday time, also decelerated, to show real terms growth of 11.0% compared with 11.7% in March.  Clearly, the economy is in less good shape than we, and others, thought, and April’s figures have dented sentiment in consequence. 

The deceleration of the economy is mainly the result of policy action aimed at cooling the housing market and at taming inflation – goals which have largely been achieved, leaving room for policy to be relaxed.  Shortly after the release of the April data, banks’ RRR was reduced by 50 basis points, to 20% for most large institutions.  This was the third such cut since December. More significantly, Premier Wen gave a clear signal in recent days that the focus of policy is switching when he stated that the government will be ‘giving more priority to maintaining growth’, while not referring to inflation. 

Thus galvanised, the pace of policy easing is likely to accelerate and we expect a range of tools to be employed: banks could well be instructed (via so-called ‘window guidance’) to channel more credit to infrastructure projects and the strategic industries identified in the Five Year Plan; new project approvals are likely to be accelerated; further cuts in the RRR are probable; tax cuts are on the cards; ‘targeted easing’ in the housing market via cheaper mortgages for first time buyers and easier access to credit for developers building small and medium sized properties is possible; and policy makers will strive to ensure the social housing completions target of 5 million units (versus 4.3 million last year) is met.  Growth-supporting policies will boost the economy directly and through the positive effect they will have on confidence.  At the same time, the government’s relatively cautious approach to date indicates that it has learnt its lessons from over stimulating the economy in 2008/09 and will take a more measured approach this time. 

Turning to the details of last month’s data, industrial production growth dropped sharply from 11.9% in March to 9.3% – the slowest rate since May 2009.  Electricity output slowed to growth of just 0.7% year-on-year, but electricity consumption fared better, with growth of 3.7%. Following March’s favourable data and indicators we had revised up our expectation for industrial production growth in the second quarter to 12.5% year-on-year, but we have now scaled that back to 10.4%.  As a result we forecast industrial output to grow by 11.8% this year and 12.4% in 2013. 

Exports were particularly weak relative to expectations in April with growth of only 4.9% – lower than any of the forecasts in a Bloomberg poll.  Exports to the USA are performing well with growth of 10%, while those to other developing economies are currently decelerating in year-on-year terms and those to the EU shrank by 2.4%.  We expect growth to pick u

p in the second half of the year as overseas markets strengthen, but it will remain very sluggish by past standards.  Imports were even more of a surprise, inching ahead by just 0.3% year-on-year which reinforced the view that domestic demand, particularly investment, is relatively weak. 

CRU International Limited confidential 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Appendix A 

151 

Fixed Asset Investment (FAI) growth slipped to 19.2% year-on-year from 21.1% the prior month, dragged lower by markedly weaker investment in transport infrastructure and in real estate.  The real estate figures appear to be a correction from a suspiciously strong start to the year and are now more in line other real estate indicators.  Real estate housing starts dropped by 14.4%  year-on-year last month and sales area by 13.4%, while growth of completions remained barely in positive territory at 0.8%.  Elevated inventories mean that already falling prices are likely to weaken further, significantly boosting affordability given that average urban incomes are rising by close to 15%. 

While investment in residential real estate will slow further, we expect investment in transport infrastructure to rally as approval and funding for new projects comes through. Investment in the power sector has already turned the corner with an increase of 19.0% so far this year following a rise of only 3.8% in 2011.  Having been a drag on growth in the second half of 2011, infrastructure investment will make a positive contribution as we move into the second half of this year. 

One of the positive aspects of last month’s data was that inflation fell to 3.4% from 3.6%, led lower by food prices.  We expect inflation to slow further due to base effects and a lagged response to slower economic growth, reaching a trough in the summer.  Not only does the more favourable inflation backdrop give space for policy easing, it is also helping the authorities reform prices further, with residential electricity tariffs to be increased from June.  Our forecast is for inflation to average 3.1% this year, rising to 3.7% next year and 4.0% thereafter; we see higher medium-term inflation as inevitable as labour shortages push up wages and as administered prices are increased to better reflect the costs of provision. 

Due to the disappointing April activity data we have edged our GDP growth forecast for this year down to 8.2% from 8.3%.  We still expect economic recovery to develop in the second half of the year and carry over into stronger growth in 2013, which we peg at 8.8%.  These forecasts are conditional, however, on the Eurozone containing its debt crisis – failure to do so poses the key downside risk to our projections.  The Chinese government is in the fortunate position of having leeway to ease both monetary and fiscal policy to counter an economic shock and we would expect it to do so.  However, the government would be unlikely to launch a stimulus package akin to that seen at the onset of the

financial crisis.  Thus GDP growth would be weaker than in our base case, with 7% a plausible lower limit.  An economic shock would alter the profile of our forecasts into the medium term but not our underlying story – trend GDP growth will slow into the medium term for structural reasons and sub-8% growth will become the norm. 

The Japanese economy appears to be stalling again after rebounding in the first three months of 2012.  Economic growth in the first quarter of 1.0% quarter-on-quarter was driven by a 1.1% quarter-on-quarter increase in private consumption, in particular of durable goods which climbed 7.4%.  Private consumption accounted for over 70% of GDP in 2010 but fell back last year as consumers delayed spending in response to the natural disasters.  While consumption has revived somewhat this year, this has largely been brought about by temporary factors such as government subsidies for fuel-efficient automobiles and reconstruction spending.

The pick-up in the first quarter owed little to trade.  Exports to China fell in the quarter by13% year-on-year and to the Eurozone by 10% year-on-year.  While exports to the USA picked up sufficiently to offset the deterioration in demand from China, the recent weakness in the US labour market and political uncertainty in Europe are risks to the future growth of exports.  The deterioration in exports is also in part due to the sustained strength of the yen, which has appreciated by almost 5% since mid-March. 

Aside from a strong currency, there are several other headwinds preventing a return to growth.  Not least of these is the uncertainty surrounding the future of energy generation.  The last of Japan’s remaining nuclear reactors went offline in early May leaving the country without nuclear energy for the first time in 40 years.  This has cast considerable doubt on the outlook for energy policy in Japan and on the economic cost of future industrial activity.  Furthermore, with exports softening and an increasing reliance on imports of expensive fossil fuels to generate replacement power, the trade deficit has widened to an historical high. 

High frequency data are not too encouraging either.  Industrial output, for example, rose by a less than expected 1.0% in March from February and manufacturers said they expected to cut output by 4.0% in May.  The deterioration in the outlook for industry was reinforced by the Markit manufacturing PMI.  The reading for April dropped off slightly from 51.1 in March to 50.7, signalling a marginally slower rate of growth in manufacturing output than the previous month, but consistent with continued, but slow recovery. 

While the pick-up in economy activity in the first quarter was encouraging, we think it is likely that growth will soften throughout the remainder of this year.  We expect domestic demand to be hit by the withdrawal of temporary spending incen

tives and the global slowdown to continue to hamper external demand.  We have therefore maintained our outlook of around 1.7% growth this year followed by around 2% annual growth throughout 2013 to 2016. 

Signs are accumulating that India’s poor economic performance in 2011 might be rolling over into 2012.  The economy remains dogged by structural issues, hampering its ability to return to high growth rates.  Interventions by authorities do not yet seem to have had the desired effects.  In terms of monetary policy, for example, last month’s interest rate cut may not yet have had much of an impact but based on the indicators highlighted below, the economy appears to be in a worse state.  Furthermore, the current account and fiscal and trade deficits remain at or around historical highs and inflation is back on the rise. 

The rupee has also come under increased pressure in recent weeks.  After a period of very steep depreciation since the beginning of February, the rupee hit an all-time low in May (above Rs 55 to the dollar).  Foreign institutional investors, following anxiety over a widening trade gap and an environment hostile to investment, pulled money out of India in April to the tune of $105 million after average inflows of $3 billion in each of the previous three months. 

Whilst a weaker currency should offer some scope for exporters to benefit, exports have recently under performed.  In April, growth in exports recovered only some ground against the fall in March, rising 3.2% year-on-year after falling 5.7% the month before. 

Elsewhere, industrial production contracted 3.5% year-on-year in March reversing almost entirely the 4.1% gain in February.  The unexpected fall in output was driven by a 21.2% yearon-year drop in capital goods and manufacturing (electrical machinery manufacturing sank

43.0% and apparel production fell 55.0%).  The manufacturing PMI, compiled by Markit, signalled little month-on-month change posting 54.9 in April from 54.7 in March.  The reading suggests that the manufacturing sector expanded at a slightly faster pace despite power outages and rising input prices.  Noticeably, there was a marked increase in the growth of new export orders. 

Although India retains relatively favourable long-term growth prospects, its near-term outlook is hampered by weak domestic activity.  Poor data are putting pressure on government to push through reforms to stimulate the economy, as does the recent ratings outlook downgrade by Standard & Poors’.  And while the poor data put pressure on the Reserve Bank of India to ease monetary policy further, a weakening currency causing a rise in inflation in April to 7.2% from 6.9% in March may limit intervention. 

We believe that India can still grow at impressive rates, but it remains to be seen whether the government has the political will to return the economy to the very high growth rates

of the mid-2000s.  We have maintained our outlook of weak growth of around 6.4% this year followed by 7.9% in 2013 and around 8.2% thereafter. 

Thailand bounced back to growth in the first quarter of 2012 after a slump in activity in the fourth quarter due to extensive flooding.  Following a 10.8% quarter-on-quarter decline in GDP in the fourth quarter, economic activity expanded by 11% quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of 2012.  Investment climbed by almost 14% quarter-on-quarter on the back of reconstruction spending.  Growth in exports was similarly impressive, rising by 11.6% quarteron-quarter, as manufacturing production resumed.  We have left our forecast broadly unchanged with growth of 4.7% this year, followed by 6.7% next year. 

Following two quarters in which economic activity contracted, GDP in Taiwan expanded by a seasonally-adjusted 1.1% quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of 2012.  The weak recovery from recession was led by consumer spending which rose 1.5% year-on-year compared with 1.0% in the fourth quarter.  We forecast growth of 2.5% this year, although given Taiwan’s high dependency on exports, weakness overseas may derail the recovery.
